name: Piazza del Campo
blurb: The shell-shaped square at the heart of Siena, paved in red brick and sloping down to the town hall, where the Palio is run.
text: The Campo lies where Siena’s three hills meet, on the old marketplace below them. The city government of the Nine had it paved in red brick from 1327 to 1349, in nine fan-shaped slices of travertine, one for each of its members, so the square opens like a shell and slopes down to the Palazzo Pubblico.

The palaces round it had to follow the same rules for their windows and their height, so the square still looks as if one hand drew it. Twice every summer it fills up with earth and people for the Palio, and on any other day the Sienese sit on its bricks in the sun.

name: Palazzo Pubblico
blurb: Siena’s Gothic town hall of brick and stone at the foot of the Campo, with the most famous frescoes of good and bad government.
text: The government of the Nine built its palace from 1297 to 1310, at the lowest point of the Campo, and it is still Siena’s town hall. Its front bends slightly to follow the curve of the square, and the black and white shield of the town sits above every arch.

Upstairs, in the Museo Civico, Simone Martini painted the Maestà in 1315, and in 1338 and 1339 Ambrogio Lorenzetti covered the room where the Nine met with the Allegory of Good and Bad Government: a busy, happy town and countryside on one wall, a ruined one on the other.

name: Torre del Mangia
blurb: The slender brick tower of the town hall, 88 metres tall, with the stone crown of its bell chamber over the Campo.
text: The Torre del Mangia went up from 1338 to 1348 beside the Palazzo Pubblico, in brick with a crown of white travertine. It stands 88 metres tall, one of the highest towers of medieval Italy, and although it rises from the lowest point of the Campo, its top stands as high as the cathedral’s bell tower on the hill.

It takes its name from its first bell ringer, Giovanni di Balduccio, who was known as Mangiaguadagni, the one who eats up his earnings. You can climb its 400 or so steps for a view over the roofs to the hills of Tuscany.

name: Fonte Gaia
blurb: The marble fountain at the top of the Campo, where the water of Siena’s underground aqueducts first reached the square.
text: Siena has no river, so it dug the bottini, kilometres of tunnels that collect the rainwater under the hills. When the water first reached the Campo in 1343 the town celebrated so much that the fountain was called the joyful one, Fonte Gaia.

Jacopo della Quercia carved its marble from 1409 to 1419, with the Virgin, the Virtues and scenes from Genesis. The worn originals are now kept in Santa Maria della Scala, and the fountain in the square is a copy that Tito Sarrocchi made in 1868.

name: Duomo di Siena
blurb: The cathedral on the highest hill of the town, striped in white and dark green marble, with a floor of inlaid marble pictures.
text: Siena’s cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta was built in the 13th century on the highest point of the town. Giovanni Pisano carved the lower half of its front from 1284, crowded with prophets and philosophers, and the bell tower and the walls inside are striped in white and dark green marble, the colours of the town’s shield.

Inside, Nicola Pisano carved the pulpit from 1265 to 1268, and Pinturicchio painted the Piccolomini Library with the life of Pope Pius II, of the Sienese family of the Piccolomini. The whole floor is a picture book of 56 marble panels, made over two centuries, which is uncovered for a few weeks every year.

name: Facciatone
blurb: The bare front of the vast new cathedral that Siena began in 1339 and gave up after the Black Death.
text: In 1339 Siena decided to build a cathedral to outdo Florence’s: the old one would become only the transept of a far bigger church. The plague of 1348 killed much of the town, the money ran out, and in 1357 the work stopped for good.

What stands of it is the Facciatone, the empty front with its tall window, and a row of arches along the side of the square. The Museo dell’Opera del Duomo now fills part of the unfinished nave, with Duccio’s Maestà, and from the top of the Facciatone you look out over the Campo and the Torre del Mangia.

name: Santa Maria della Scala
blurb: One of the oldest hospitals of Europe, opposite the cathedral, which looked after pilgrims and foundlings for nearly a thousand years.
text: Santa Maria della Scala took in the pilgrims on the Via Francigena, the sick and the abandoned children of Siena from the 11th century until the end of the 20th, when the hospital moved out of town. It is now a museum, a small town of halls, chapels and cellars under the cathedral square.

In the Pellegrinaio, the long ward of the pilgrims, Domenico di Bartolo and others painted the hospital’s own work in the 1440s: feeding the poor, nursing the sick, raising the foundlings. The original panels of the Fonte Gaia are kept here too.

name: Loggia della Mercanzia
blurb: The 15th-century loggia of the merchants’ court, at the crossing where Siena’s three main streets meet above the Campo.
text: At the Croce del Travaglio, the crossing of Banchi di Sopra, Banchi di Sotto and Via di Città, the three roads from the three thirds of the town meet. Here the Mercanzia, the court that settled the merchants’ quarrels, built its loggia from 1417, with statues of saints on its pillars.
From under its arches a few steps lead down to the Campo, and the whole of Siena passes in front of it in the evening.

name: Piazza Salimbeni
blurb: The small square of the palaces of the Monte dei Paschi, the oldest bank in the world still in business.
text: The Monte dei Paschi di Siena was set up in 1472 to lend money to the poor at fair interest, and it has worked ever since, which makes it the oldest bank in the world. It has its seat in the Gothic Palazzo Salimbeni, at the back of this square on Banchi di Sopra.
Beside it stand the Renaissance Palazzo Spannocchi and the Palazzo Tantucci, and in the middle the statue of Sallustio Bandini, the Sienese priest who argued for free trade in the 18th century.

name: San Domenico
blurb: The great brick church of the Dominicans on its own hill, where Saint Catherine of Siena prayed, and where her head is kept.
text: The Dominicans started building their church in 1226, a long, plain barn of brick on the hill west of the centre, with a view across the valley of Fontebranda to the cathedral.

Catherine Benincasa, the daughter of a wool dyer from the quarter below it, prayed here. She talked popes and princes into peace, brought the pope back to Rome from Avignon, and became a patron saint of Italy and of Europe. In a chapel inside, her head is kept in a reliquary, and a portrait of her by Andrea Vanni, said to be the only one painted in her lifetime, hangs on the wall.

name: Fortezza Medicea
blurb: The fortress that Florence built after it took Siena in 1555, now a park on its walls above the town.
text: After a siege of more than a year Siena gave in to the army of Florence and of the emperor in 1555, and it lost the freedom it had kept for four centuries. From 1561 Cosimo I de’ Medici had this fortress of four bastions built, to keep the town in check.
Today its walls are a park, where the Sienese go for a walk or a run, with a view over the towers and the green of La Lizza beside it.

name: Palio di Siena
blurb: The wild horse race round the Campo, run twice every summer between the contrade, the neighbourhoods of the town.
text: Siena is split into seventeen contrade, each with its own animal, colours, church, fountain and museum. On 2 July and on 16 August ten of them race in the Palio: three laps round the Campo, bareback, on a track of earth laid over the bricks, in about a minute and a half. A horse that has thrown its jockey can still win.

Days of trials, blessings of the horses in the contrade’s churches and a parade in medieval dress lead up to it. The winner takes the drappellone, a silk banner painted for each race, and the whole contrada celebrates for weeks.

name: Panforte
blurb: Siena’s dense cake of honey, almonds, candied fruit and spices, baked here since the Middle Ages.
text: Panforte, the strong bread, is a flat, chewy cake of honey and sugar with almonds, candied orange and melon and a lot of spice, the way the Sienese apothecaries made it in the Middle Ages. The dark panpepato has pepper in it too.

The white Panforte Margherita, covered in icing sugar, was made in 1879 for Queen Margherita’s visit. Siena also bakes the soft almond biscuits called ricciarelli, and both are sold in every pastry shop on Banchi di Sopra.
